title: Orchestrator egress pin failure during agent upgrade caused intermittent control-plane disconnects
creator: Marco R. Silva
description:
Summary:

During a scheduled agent/sidecar upgrade in Private clusters (rolling upgrade across customer VPCs) we observed repeated, intermittent control-plane disconnects for a subset (~12%) of agents. Symptoms included authentication failures (TLS handshake errors), high reconnect rates in the orchestrator, elevated control-plane CPU, and a surge in ephemeral port usage on the egress NATs. The outage window lasted ~32 minutes for affected customers while mitigation proceeded.

Why this ticket exists:
This ticket captures the post-incident investigation findings, root cause analysis, temporary and permanent mitigations, and prioritized action items to prevent recurrence in future upgrades. It is intentionally focused on the interaction between local DNS caching, egress IP pinning, and orchestrator endpoint rotation during agent lifecycle events.
timeline:
2026-03-01T02:05Z - Upgrade job started (canary cohort).
2026-03-01T02:09Z - On-call alerted to increased control-plane TLS handshake failures for canary cohort.
2026-03-01T02:11Z - Metrics: orchestrator reconnect rate x15 baseline, control-plane auth errors spike. Grafana: dashboards/expr/CP-AuthErrors.
2026-03-01T02:12Z - Partial mitigation: roll back canary cohort upgrade; new canaries still showing failures.
2026-03-01T02:18Z - SRE added temporary iptables SNAT rule to force egress through primary NAT (mitigated port exhaustion symptoms).
2026-03-01T02:20Z - Observed that failed agents were resolving control-plane DNS to old leader A-records due to local resolver cache TTLs; some continued to connect to decommissioned leader IPs that had been removed from the service LB.
2026-03-01T02:26Z - Temporary remediation: forced DNS cache flush and increased orchestrator dial timeout/backoff. Incident declared resolved at ~2026-03-01T02:37Z as reconnect rates returned to baseline.
observations:
- Agents that failed had egress pinned IPs that coincidentally mapped to the decommissioned control-plane leader network path.
- DNS changes propagated at the LB layer but client-side caches (glibc/resolv) had stale A records for up to TTL seconds; some inlined DNS libraries kept older entries longer during ongoing connections.
- NAT ephemeral port exhaustion exacerbated reconnects when agents retried quickly.
- Orchestrator health checks did not detect a subset of connections using 'stale path' because their local connection attempts produced TLS errors before application-level retries.
- Control-plane high CPU was primarily due to auth handshake retries and session state rebuilds from reconnect storms.
root_cause: A confluence of three factors: (1) rolling change to control-plane endpoint allocation during the upgrade window, (2) client-side DNS caches and resolver library behavior retaining old A records longer than expected, and (3) egress NAT ephemeral port pressure causing retries to fail faster and spread reconnect impact. The orchestrator lacked a gating check to prevent agents from simultaneously re-resolving and re-initiating connections in a way that amplified load on a shrinking set of endpoints.
mitigations_taken:
- Immediate: rolled back latest agent image for affected cohorts; forced DNS cache flush on coordinator nodes; applied temporary SNAT iptables rule to stabilize egress semantics.
- Short-term (during incident): slowed agent reconnect backoff to reduce connection storming; added synthetic health endpoints to divert some auth validation traffic.
- Monitoring: created ad-hoc Grafana panels for NAT port utilization and DNS resolution variance per AZ.
action_items: AI-1: Add a pre-upgrade gating check in the orchestrator to verify canonical control-plane endpoint set consistency across all AZs before proceeding with agent upgrades. (owner: Aisha Patel, estimate: 3, due: 2026-03-21)

AI-2: Implement a server-side connection draining window with DNS TTL coordination: when control-plane endpoints are removed, delay removal by TTL + safety margin and emit a deprecation header to clients. (owner: Yun Park, estimate: 5, due: 2026-04-04)
AI-3: Instrument and alert on per-cluster DNS resolution divergence (percent of agents resolving to non-primary IPs) and expose as SLO/guardrail. (owner: SRE Team, estimate: 3, due: 2026-03-28)

AI-4: Harden agent resolver behavior: on upgrade, prefer fresh A/AAAA lookups and implement an aggressive cache invalidation path when instructed by orchestrator. (owner: Eng-Agent, estimate: 8, due: 2026-04-11)
AI-5: Increase ephemeral port headroom on NAT gateways for rolling upgrades and implement per-upgrade port reservation if feasible. (owner: Infra-Networking, estimate: 5, due: 2026-03-30)
AI-6: Add runbook steps for on-call including: how to flush agent DNS caches remotely, how to apply temporary SNAT rule, and when to pause upgrades. (owner: Oncall Lead, estimate: 2, due: 2026-03-18)
AI-7: Postmortem doc: write a customer-facing incident summary and include mitigations offered to affected customers. (owner: PM - Serena Liu, estimate: 1, due: 2026-03-16)
AI-8: Review and add unit/integration tests that simulate DNS A record rotation + NAT port scarcity to catch similar regressions in CI. (owner: QA, estimate: 5, due: 2026-04-08)
decisions:
- We will not change global default DNS TTLs. Instead we will coordinate endpoint removal with a departure window and improve client cache invalidation hooks.
- Orchestrator upgrades will require a 'no-divergence' check where at least 95% of live agents resolve the same endpoint set before proceeding beyond the canary stage.
